It's rarely a sudden loss of ability. Chemistry is one of the most
cumulative
subjects in the BC curriculum — each unit quietly assumes you fully understood the last one. In Chemistry 11 you meet the mole, stoichiometry, and how atoms bond. In Chemistry 12 you're expected to
use

all of that fluently while learning reaction kinetics, chemical equilibrium, acids and bases, and solubility. If the foundation from Chem 11 was a little shaky — memorised rather than understood — Chem 12 is where those small cracks become a visible drop in the grade.

concept gaps that compound

The Mole: The Idea Everything Else Quietly Stands On

If we had to name the single concept that decides whether Chemistry 11 and 12 feel easy or impossible, it's the mole. It sounds simple — a counting unit — but students who "kind of" get it end up guessing their way through every calculation that follows.
The mole connects three things: the number of particles, the mass you can weigh on a scale, and (for gases) the volume. Avogadro's number is the bridge:
1 mole = 6.022 × 10²³ particles
moles (n) = mass (m) / molar mass (M)
Once that clicks, stoichiometry stops being scary. Take a classic Chem 11 problem: how many grams of water form when 4.0 g of hydrogen react completely with oxygen?
2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O
mole ratio H₂ : H₂O = 2 : 2 = 1 : 1, so n(H₂O) ≈ 1.98 mol
mass(H₂O) = 1.98 mol × 18.02 g/mol ≈ 35.7 g
A student who
understands

the mole sees the balanced equation as a recipe of ratios. A student who memorised a procedure freezes the moment the numbers change. That difference is exactly what we diagnose and fix. We explain more about the memorisation trap on our
blog
, because it shows up in every science subject.
Equilibrium and Kinetics: Where Chem 12 Separates the Class

Chemistry 12 introduces the topics that many BC students find genuinely hard for the first time: reaction kinetics and chemical equilibrium. These aren't harder because the math is scarier — it's because they demand you hold a
dynamic
picture in your head.

Equilibrium is not "the reaction stopped." It's forward and reverse reactions running at equal rates. Students who memorise the equilibrium constant expression but don't picture that balance can't reason through Le Chatelier's principle when a question changes the pressure or temperature. The expression itself is straightforward once the idea underneath is solid:
For aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD:  Keq = ([C]ᶜ · [D]ᵈ) / ([A]ᵃ · [B]ᵇ)
The
meaning

is what matters: a large Keq means products are favoured; a small one means reactants dominate. When we tutor Chem 12 equilibrium, we spend time on that intuition first, because every ICE-table problem and every "which way does the shift go?" question flows from it.
Kinetics is similar — it's about
why

concentration, temperature, and catalysts change reaction speed, connected to collision theory. Memorise the graphs and you'll stumble; understand collisions and activation energy and the graphs read themselves.
Acids, Bases, and the pH Panic

The acid–base and solubility units near the end of Chem 12 are where the exam pressure — "the fog before the exam," as one student put it — hits hardest. There's a lot of new vocabulary, and it arrives when the year is already busy.
The core tool is simpler than it looks:
pH = −log[H⁺]   and   [H⁺] · [OH⁻] = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ (at 25°C)

So a solution with [H⁺] = 1.0 × 10⁻³ mol/L has a pH of 3 — acidic. A student who understands that logarithm as "each pH unit is a ten-fold change in acidity" reasons confidently; one who memorised a button-press sequence on the calculator gets lost the moment a question is phrased differently.

1. Stoichiometry and the Mole
Everything in chemistry runs through the mole, and if that foundation is shaky, nothing downstream holds. The core relationship students must own — not memorise, own — is:

Integers (negative numbers), ratios, early algebraic thinking, and the bridge into the abstraction that Grade 8 demands.

children.text: When Your Child Can Read the Words but Miss the Meaning

Here's a scene many Metro Vancouver parents know well. Your child reads a page aloud smoothly — every word crisp, no stumbles. You ask, "So what just happened in the story?" and you get a shrug. Or a guess. Or a retelling of the
last
sentence and nothing before it.
That gap — reading the words but not holding the meaning — is one of the most common (and most misunderstood) struggles we see in K–7 students. It's easy to assume it's a
reading
problem. Usually, it isn't. Your child can decode just fine. What's missing is
comprehension
: the invisible work of turning strings of words into a picture, an idea, a sequence they can actually talk about.

The good news? Comprehension isn't a fixed trait a child either has or doesn't. It's a set of teachable skills — and small gaps in those skills tend to compound quietly until a Grade 4 or 5 assignment suddenly feels impossible. As a PhD-led practice, our whole approach is built on finding the
specific
gap rather than throwing more reading at the problem and hoping.

— no pressure.
Decoding vs. Comprehension: The Distinction That Changes Everything
Reading is really two jobs happening at once. Reading researchers describe it with a simple, well-established idea called the
Simple View of Reading
Reading Comprehension = Decoding × Language Comprehension
Notice it's a
product
, not a sum. That multiplication sign matters enormously. If either factor is near zero, the whole thing collapses — even if the other is strong.
A child with strong
decoding
but weak
language comprehension
reads fluently out loud but can't tell you what it meant (this is the "reads-but-doesn't-get-it" child).
A child with strong
language comprehension
but weak
decoding
understands stories perfectly when
you
read to them, but stumbles when reading alone.
Most worried parents assume their child is in the second group and drill phonics harder. But a huge number of K–7 students are actually in the
first
group — fluent decoders whose comprehension quietly stalled. Drilling more reading speed does nothing for them. You have to build the comprehension side directly.
This is exactly the kind of misdiagnosis our approach is designed to catch. In the same way we teach science by fixing
concept gaps
rather than pushing memorisation — something we write about often on our
blog
— we teach reading by finding
which
factor is holding a child back, then working on that one.
The Five Skills Hiding Inside "Good Comprehension"
When a child "understands what they read," they're actually doing five distinct things almost invisibly. When comprehension breaks down, it's usually one or two of these — not all of them.
Vocabulary
— knowing enough words that meaning doesn't stall. A single unknown key word can fog an entire paragraph.
Background knowledge
— you can't comprehend a passage about tide pools if you've never encountered the idea of tides. Comprehension is knowledge-dependent.
Sentence structure (syntax)
— understanding
who did what to whom
, especially in longer or reordered sentences ("The girl the dog chased was laughing").
Making inferences
— reading between the lines, connecting a cause on page 2 to an effect on page 5.
Comprehension monitoring
— noticing
when you've stopped understanding
and going back. Strong readers do this automatically; struggling readers plough on, lost.
Here's the crucial part for parents: a child can look like a "weak reader" when really they have four strong skills and one weak one. A
one-on-one reading comprehension tutor in Vancouver

can isolate which skill is the bottleneck — and that changes the entire plan. It's the difference between "read more" (vague, frustrating) and "let's work on catching yourself when you lose the thread" (specific, learnable).
How the BC Curriculum Raises the Bar — Especially Around Grade 4

BC's redesigned English Language Arts curriculum expects steadily more sophisticated comprehension as children move through the grades. In the early years (K–3), the emphasis is on decoding and simple story recall. Then something shifts.
Educators often describe it as the move from
"learning to read" to "reading to learn."
Around Grades 4 and 5, children stop reading mostly simple stories and start reading to
acquire information
— in science, social studies, and math word problems. Suddenly comprehension isn't just for English class; it's the tool for
everything

This is why so many parents in Burnaby, Coquitlam, Richmond, and across Metro Vancouver come to us saying their child was "fine until Grade 4." Nothing went wrong — the demands simply changed, and a comprehension gap that was invisible in Grade 2 became visible when the reading got denser.
Even math is affected. Consider a typical Grade 5 word problem:
A recipe needs (3) / (4) cup of flour per batch. For 3 batches you need (3) / (4) × 3 = (9) / (4) = 2¼ cups.
A child who "can't do the math" here often
can
do the math — they couldn't decode what the words were asking. Comprehension is the hidden gatekeeper of math word problems too, which is one reason our reading and
K–7 math
support so often reinforce each other.

Book a free, no-pressure assessment
and we'll show you — in plain language, with a real plan.
The Understanding-First Method: How We Actually Rebuild Comprehension
We don't hand a child a worksheet and mark it. We teach the
thinking process
that strong readers use, out loud, until it becomes the child's own habit. A few of the strategies we lean on:
Think-alouds.
The tutor narrates their own reading thoughts — "Wait, I don't know what
migrate
means. Let me use the rest of the sentence to guess." This makes the invisible work of comprehension
visible
, so the child can copy it.
Retell and summarise.
After each chunk, the child says what happened in their own words. This is the single fastest way to catch comprehension breakdowns — because you can't summarise what you didn't understand.
Question generation.
We teach children to ask
their own
questions of a text ("Why did the character do that?"). Curious readers comprehend better, because they're reading with a purpose.
Explicit inference practice.
We slow down at exactly the moments where meaning lives between the lines — the cause on one page, the consequence three pages later.
Comprehension monitoring.
Perhaps the most important habit: teaching a child to
notice the fog
and stop, reread, and repair. Skilled readers do this constantly and unconsciously; we make it deliberate first, then automatic.

Because ours is a PhD-led practice, this method is set and overseen to a consistent standard, then delivered one-on-one by qualified tutors — in-person in Burnaby or online across Metro Vancouver. Sessions run comfortably from Vancouver, New Westminster, Surrey, North Vancouver and beyond, so you're never limited by a commute. You can read more about
choosing in-person vs. online tutoring
when you're deciding what fits your family.
What You Can Do at Home Tonight (No Tutor Required)
Comprehension grows fastest when school, tutoring, and home pull in the same direction. A few genuinely effective, research-aligned habits:
Read
with
them, not just
to
them.
Pause and wonder aloud: "Hmm, why do you think she did that?" You're modelling comprehension monitoring.
Ask "how do you know?"
When your child answers a question, ask them to point to the words that told them. This builds the evidence-and-inference muscle.
Talk about ideas, not just plot.
"What would
you
have done?" turns passive reading into active thinking.
Front-load background knowledge.
Before a book about the ocean, watch a short clip or chat about the beach. Comprehension is easier when the topic isn't brand new.
Let them re-read favourites.
Re-reading builds fluency
and
deepens comprehension — it's not wasted time.

None of this requires special materials — just a few intentional minutes and a curious tone. The goal isn't to quiz your child into anxiety; it's to make thinking-about-reading a normal, low-stakes part of the day.
Why Small Comprehension Gaps Compound — and Why Early Help Matters

There's a well-documented pattern in reading development where strong early readers read more, learn more words, and pull further ahead — while struggling readers read less, and the gap widens. Researchers call it the "Matthew Effect" (the rich get richer).
The takeaway for parents isn't panic — it's timing. Comprehension gaps are highly fixable, and they're
easiest

to fix before a child decides "I'm just bad at reading" and starts avoiding it. Confidence and comprehension feed each other: a child who understands what they read enjoys it, reads more, and improves faster.

That's really the heart of what we do — we turn "I hate reading" back into "I get it now." Not through pressure or drilling, but by fixing the specific understanding gap underneath the frustration. When the
why
finally clicks, the next book isn't a fresh battle.
Bringing It Together: A Plan That Fits Your Child

Every child's comprehension profile is different. One needs vocabulary and background knowledge; another needs to slow down and catch themselves when the fog rolls in; another simply needs the confidence to trust their own thinking. There's no single worksheet that fixes all of them — which is exactly why a one-on-one, diagnosis-first approach works where generic programs stall.

a concept out loud, not just solve a problem. If they can compute an answer but can't tell you why the method works, that's a memorisation habit masking a concept gap. Our

Habit 1: Practise Retrieval, Not Re-Reading
The single most powerful study habit is also the most uncomfortable:
retrieval practice

. Instead of rereading notes, close the book and try to reconstruct the idea from memory. The struggle to recall is what actually builds the memory — cognitive scientists call this the "desirable difficulty."
Here's the concrete version for a Chemistry 11 student learning stoichiometry. Don't reread the worked example — cover it and solve from scratch:
2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O
If you start with 5.0 mol of H₂, how much water forms? A retrieval-trained student reasons through the mole ratio without peeking:
(5.0 mol H₂) × (2 mol H₂O) / (2 mol H₂) = 5.0 mol H₂O
The student who
reread
the example recognises it; the student who
retrieved
it can do the next, unfamiliar version on the exam. That's the entire game.
Habit 2: Space It Out (The Forgetting Curve Is Your Friend)

Studying all of Biology 12 the night before the provincial is the academic equivalent of watering a plant once a month with a fire hose. Spaced practice — short, revisited sessions over days and weeks — dramatically outperforms one long cram.
The reason is the forgetting curve: memory decays predictably, but each time you retrieve information
just
as you're about to forget it, the decay slows. Three 25-minute sessions across a week beat one exhausting three-hour block, every time.

Monday:

Wednesday:

Friday:
teach the concept out loud to a parent or sibling — teaching exposes gaps instantly.
Following week:
mix it into a short review with older topics (this is "interleaving").

study-skills blog
Habit 3: Interleave Topics So Skills Transfer
Most textbooks block practice by topic: ten kinematics problems in a row, then ten force problems. Students feel fluent — but that fluency is fake, because they always know
which
method to use. On a real Physics 12 exam, problems arrive shuffled.
Interleaving
— mixing problem types in one session — trains the harder, more valuable skill of
choosing
the right approach. It feels worse in the moment (accuracy dips during practice) and produces far better exam performance.

identify and set up

Δx = v₀t + ½at²
A ball dropped from rest (v₀ = 0) for 2.0 s falls:

The interleaved student sees the words "dropped from rest" and instantly knows v₀ = 0 and which equation applies — because they've practised distinguishing it from a projectile or constant-velocity problem, not drilling it in isolation.

Habit 4: Diagnose the Error Type, Not Just the Wrong Answer
When a student loses marks, the lazy fix is "be more careful." Effective academic coaching asks a sharper question:
what kind
of error was that?
Concept error:
they didn't understand the underlying idea. (Fix: reteach the foundation.)
Procedure error:
they knew the idea but slipped in the steps. (Fix: slow, structured practice.)
Careless error:
they knew and could do it, but rushed. (Fix: checking routines, not more content.)

Most students and parents lump all three together as "silly mistakes." They're not the same, and they need completely different remedies. A student drowning in concept errors doesn't need more practice sheets — that just reinforces the misunderstanding. This diagnostic step is exactly what a PhD-led method is built to do well: find the

This matters enormously for exam prep. On BC Provincial numeracy assessments and the SAT, the difference between a 78% and an 88% is often not new knowledge — it's eliminating one repeated careless pattern. Our

Habit 5: Build a Confidence Loop, Not a Panic Spiral
Grades and confidence feed each other — in both directions. A student who understands
why
a method works walks in calm; a student running on memorisation walks in braced for the fog. Anxiety then eats working memory during the exam, which causes the exact blank-out they feared.

The fix isn't a pep talk. It's competence. When a student genuinely understands orgo reaction mechanisms — instead of memorising 40 disconnected arrows — the exam stops being a memory test and becomes a reasoning task they can actually navigate. Confidence follows understanding; it can't be installed the other way around.
This is why we never lead with "we'll get you an A." We can't honestly promise a number. What we

If you've heard your teenager mutter "it's just not clicking" while staring at a page of hexagons and curved arrows — or if you're a UBC or SFU student watching your first orgo midterm approach with a growing fog of dread — you're in very familiar territory. Organic chemistry has a reputation as a "weeder" course for a reason. But that reputation is mostly built on a misunderstanding of how the subject actually works.

Here's the thing most students discover too late: organic chemistry is the subject where memorisation fails hardest. There are hundreds of reactions, and if you try to survive by flashcarding each one, you'll drown. The students who thrive learn to see the
logic
underneath — a small set of rules about how electrons behave, applied over and over. Once you understand
why

The Real Reason Orgo Breaks Students (It's Not Ability)
Most struggle in organic chemistry isn't a lack of intelligence. It's a foundation problem that compounds quietly.

Here's how it happens. A student misses a subtle point about electronegativity or how a lone pair behaves. It seems minor. But three weeks later, that gap makes resonance structures confusing. Two weeks after that, the confusing resonance makes it impossible to see why a certain carbon is electrophilic. foundation underneath them

Mechanisms Made Clear: Arrow-Pushing Is a Logic, Not a List
Let's get concrete, because this is where the real learning lives.
The curved arrow in organic chemistry means one thing:
the movement of a pair of electrons

Take a classic

Nu⁻ + R−CH₂−LG → Nu−CH₂−R + LG⁻
The nucleophile (Nu⁻) brings a lone pair, attacks the carbon from the side opposite the leaving group, and the C−LG bond breaks as the Nu−C bond forms. Understanding
why

The rate of an Sₙ2 reaction depends on
both

rate = k · [substrate] · [nucleophile]
Contrast that with an

only
rate = k · [substrate]

A student who has memorised these as two disconnected facts will mix them up under exam pressure. A student who understands that Sₙ1 has a slow first step forming the carbocation — so only that step controls the rate — will never confuse them. That's the whole game: understand the
why

We apply the same lens to acid-base chemistry, which quietly governs half of orgo. When we compare acid strength, we use pKₐ and the simple truth that a lower pKₐ means a stronger acid:
pKₐ = −log₁₀(Kₐ)

A student who really understands that a stable conjugate base makes a strong acid can reason through problems they've never seen before. That's the confidence we're building toward — and it's why our students stop dreading the exam and start recognising the patterns.

children.text: The Student Who Knows It All — Until the Exam Starts

Every term, we meet a certain kind of student here in Burnaby. They do the homework. They can explain the concept to you at the kitchen table on a Tuesday. Then the exam lands, the clock starts, and something goes wrong — the mind goes blank, the easy question suddenly looks unfamiliar, and they leave the room knowing they underperformed. Parents describe it the same way every time:
"She actually understands the material — so why does the grade not show it?"
That gap between what a student knows and what they can
produce under exam conditions
is exactly what exam strategy coaching addresses. It isn't more content. It isn't more cramming. It's the missing layer between understanding a subject and demonstrating it when it counts.

At Dr. Shreyank Educare, we're a PhD-led practice, and our whole method is built on one idea: most exam struggles aren't a knowledge problem at all. Why Capable Students Still Freeze: The Real Diagnosis
When a student who "knows it" bombs a test, there are usually three causes hiding underneath — and they're often mistaken for each other.
1. Concept gaps that only show under pressure.
A student can follow a worked example in a calm setting because the structure is already on the page. Strip that scaffolding away on a test, and a shaky foundation gives out. If someone memorised
how
to do stoichiometry without understanding
why

the mole ratios work, they can survive homework but stall the moment a question is phrased differently. This is why we always diagnose the underlying understanding first — the symptom is the low exam grade, but the cause is the gap.
2. No process for the exam itself.

Knowledge and test-taking are two different skills. Reading a whole exam before starting, budgeting minutes per mark, deciding when to skip and return, showing work for method marks — none of that is taught in most classrooms. Students are expected to absorb it by osmosis, and many never do.
3. Genuine exam stress.

The physiological "fog before the exam" is real. A racing heart and a blank mind aren't a character flaw; they're a stress response that a student can be trained to manage. When they have a plan, the panic has less room to grow.
Good exam strategy coaching works on all three at once. You can read more about how we separate these in our post on
concept gaps versus practice gaps
The Method: Diagnose the Gap, Then Build the Process
We start every coaching relationship with a diagnosis, not a lecture. Before we talk strategy, we find out
where

a student actually loses marks. Is it the first few questions (a slow, anxious start)? The long-answer problems (a method gap)? The last 20 minutes (poor time budgeting)? The pattern tells us what to build.
Once we know the shape of the problem, we build a repeatable exam process. For a two-hour BC provincial or a UBC midterm, that might look like:
Survey first (2–3 minutes):
read the whole paper, note the marks per section, and mentally flag the quick wins.
Budget by marks, not by order:
if a question is worth 6 of 60 marks in a 60-minute exam, it deserves roughly 6 minutes — no more. Do the easy marks first.
Show method, always:
in BC science and math, method marks are real. A student who writes the correct formula and substitution earns marks even with an arithmetic slip.
Leave a review buffer:
the last 5–8 minutes are for checking units, signs, and the questions you flagged to return to.
A reset ritual for the fog:
a slow breath, one re-read, and starting with a question you're confident about to build momentum.

This process becomes second nature through practice under realistic conditions — timed, with real past-paper questions from the actual curriculum a student is sitting. Time Budgeting Is Math — So Let's Treat It Like Math
Most students never do the arithmetic that would calm them down. Exam time is a resource you allocate, and the calculation is simple.
If you have T minutes and an exam worth M total marks, the time you should spend per mark is:
minutes per mark = T ÷ M
For a 90-minute exam worth 100 marks:
90 ÷ 100 = 0.9 minutes per mark ≈ 54 seconds per mark

Knowing this in advance changes behaviour. A student who has silently spent 25 minutes on a 12-mark question — and left 40 marks untouched — didn't lack knowledge; they lacked a budget. We teach students to glance at the mark value and immediately know their ceiling. It's a small habit that recovers a startling number of lost marks.
Worked Example: Where Marks Actually Live in Science Exams

Exam strategy isn't abstract — it's most powerful when it meets the real content. Consider a classic BC Chemistry 11/12 question on stoichiometry. Students who memorised a procedure freeze when the numbers change; students who understand the
why
stay calm.
Suppose you're asked how many grams of water form when 4.0 g of hydrogen reacts fully with oxygen:
2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O
The strategy is to work in moles, not grams. First convert:
moles H₂ = (4.0 g) ÷ (2.0 g/mol) = 2.0 mol
The balanced equation shows a 2 : 2 ratio between H₂ and H₂O, so:
moles H₂O = 2.0 mol
mass H₂O = 2.0 mol × 18.0 g/mol = 36 g
Every arrow in that chain is a method mark. A student who writes the balanced equation, the mole conversion, and the ratio earns most of the marks

The same logic applies in Physics 11/12. On a kinematics question, writing the correct equation before plugging in numbers protects your marks:

Students who leap straight to a number and get it wrong score zero. Students trained to lay out the equation, substitute, then solve, capture partial credit and — just as importantly — think more clearly. We coach this habit across

Managing the Fog: Exam Stress Isn't a Weakness
When a student says "my mind just went blank," they're describing a real stress response, not a lack of preparation. The good news: it's trainable.
The most reliable antidote is
familiarity

So we make the exam feel known — through timed past papers, so the format holds no surprises; through a fixed opening ritual, so the first two minutes are on autopilot; and through starting on a confident question, so the brain gets an early "I can do this" signal before tackling harder material.

after school science tutor Vancouver

When a student says "I'm just not a science person," it's almost never true. In our experience across hundreds of sessions, struggle in science comes down to two things:
concept gaps
and
memorisation masking a shaky foundation
A concept gap is a small piece of understanding that got skipped or half-learned — and because science builds on itself, that small gap compounds. A student who never truly understood
what a mole is

will white-knuckle their way through balancing equations, get the right answer sometimes, and completely fall apart when the problem is worded differently. The grade says "careless." The reality is a foundation with a crack in it.
Memorisation is the other trap. Biology is the classic example — students try to survive cell respiration or Mendelian genetics by memorising terms, and it works right up until the exam asks them to
apply
the idea. Then the memorised list evaporates. Real understanding is what survives the pressure of an exam; memorised facts are what create "the fog" the night before.
An after-school science tutor who only re-explains the current homework treats the symptom. The better approach — and the one our PhD-led practice is built around — is to find the
original

Physics: Where Understanding One Equation Unlocks the Whole Unit
Physics 11 and 12 in BC frustrate students because they look like a giant list of formulas to memorise. They aren't. Most of a unit flows from a handful of core relationships — once a student
understands
those, they stop memorising and start reasoning.
Take kinematics, usually the first big hurdle in Physics 11. The equation students dread is:
v² = v₀² + 2·a·Δx
Where v is final velocity, v₀ is initial velocity, a is acceleration, and Δx is displacement. A memoriser plugs numbers in and hopes. A student who
understands

it sees a story: this equation connects speed and distance when you don't know the time. Once that clicks, they know exactly when to reach for it — and that's the difference between a B and genuine command of the material.
Same with Newton's second law, the backbone of the entire forces unit:
Fₙₑₜ = m·a → written cleanly: ΣF = m·a
Every force problem — friction, tension, an object on an incline — is a variation on this one idea. We teach students to draw the free-body diagram first,
understand

what forces are actually acting, and then the math becomes almost automatic. A physics tutor's job isn't to solve the problem for them; it's to make the reasoning visible so they can solve the next one alone.
Chemistry: The Mole, Stoichiometry, and Why Grade 11 Is the Fork in the Road

Chemistry 11 is where a lot of Metro Vancouver students quietly decide whether they "like" chemistry — and it usually hinges on one concept: the mole. If the mole never truly clicks, stoichiometry becomes a nightmare, and Chemistry 12 (with equilibrium and acids-bases) becomes nearly impossible.
Stoichiometry is really just careful bookkeeping once you understand the mole ratio. Consider the combustion of methane:
CH₄ + 2 O₂ → CO₂ + 2 H₂O
The coefficients tell you the ratio: 1 mole of CH₄ reacts with 2 moles of O₂. If you start with 3.0 moles of methane, you need:
3.0 mol CH₄ × (2 mol O₂ / 1 mol CH₄) = 6.0 mol O₂
That's the entire logic of stoichiometry — a ratio, applied carefully. Students who memorise steps get lost the moment a problem adds grams or limiting reactants. Students who
understand
the ratio can handle any version. We spend the time to make that foundation solid, because everything downstream depends on it.
The same is true for
Organic Chemistry

why
mechanisms flow the way they do, the reactions stop being random. If your student is heading into or struggling with orgo, our

seems

apply
concepts, and memorised lists don't apply.
Genetics is the perfect example. A monohybrid cross between two heterozygous parents (Aa × Aa) produces the classic ratio:
Genotype: 1 AA : 2 Aa : 1 aa
Phenotype: 3 dominant : 1 recessive
A student who memorised "3:1" is stuck the moment the question involves a dihybrid cross or a test cross. A student who
understands
why that ratio emerges — because each parent passes one allele, independently — can build a Punnett square for any cross and reason their way through. That's the durable skill.
Senior biology students sometimes even meet the chi-square test to check whether observed results match expected ratios:
χ² = Σ (O − E)² / E
Where O is the observed count and E is the expected count. It looks intimidating, but it's just a structured way of asking "how far off from expected are we?" When a tutor unpacks the
meaning

children.text: Why Course Selection Is One of the Most Important Decisions You'll Make in High School

Here's something families in Burnaby and across Metro Vancouver often discover too late: the courses you choose in Grade 10, 11, and 12 quietly decide which doors stay open at UBC, SFU, and beyond. A single missing prerequisite can rule out a program before a student has even applied.
That sounds stressful — but it doesn't have to be. Good
course selection guidance in BC
isn't about panicking over every checkbox. It's about understanding how the BC curriculum connects to your goals, so you choose with confidence instead of guessing.
We talk to parents every year who say the same thing:
"We didn't realise Pre-Calculus 12 was required for that program."

Or the student who took the harder science thinking it looked good — and lost the grade point average that actually mattered for admission. These aren't rare stories. They're the predictable result of choosing courses without a map.

This guide is that map. We'll walk through how BC's graduation requirements work, how the math and science pathways branch, what universities actually ask for, and how to sequence courses so each year builds on the last. As a PhD-led practice, our whole philosophy is that understanding beats memorisation — and that applies to planning your high school just as much as it applies to a chemistry exam.

How BC Graduation Requirements Actually Work (The Part Nobody Explains Clearly)
To graduate with a
BC Dogwood Diploma
, students complete a set of required and elective courses across Grades 10–12, totalling a minimum of 80 credits. Most courses are worth 4 credits each.
The required areas include:
Language Arts
— English Studies 10, plus a Grade 11 and a Grade 12 language arts course
Mathematics
— a Math 10, plus a Math 11 (or 12)
Science
— a Science 10, plus a Grade 11 or 12 science
Social Studies
— Social Studies 10, plus a Grade 11 or 12 social studies
Physical & Health Education 10
Arts Education and/or Applied Design, Skills and Technologies (ADST) 10–12
, and
Career-Life Education / Career-Life Connections
Students also complete provincial assessments: the
Grade 10 Numeracy Assessment
, the
Grade 10 Literacy Assessment
, and the
Grade 12 Literacy Assessment
. These are graduation requirements — you don't get a percentage grade, but you must complete them.
Here's the catch that trips families up:
graduating
and
qualifying for the university program you want

are two different bars. The Dogwood minimum is the floor. Competitive university programs sit well above it. So course selection is really two questions at once — "What do I need to graduate?" and "What do I need for where I want to go next?"
Getting comfortable with the underlying math and science before Grade 11 makes those higher bars far more reachable. Our
high school subject support for Grades 8–12
is built exactly around closing those foundational gaps early.
The Math Fork in the Road: Pre-Calculus, Foundations, or Both?
Math is where the most consequential — and most misunderstood — choices happen. After
Foundations of Mathematics and Pre-Calculus 10
, the BC pathway splits into three Grade 11 streams:
Pre-Calculus 11 & 12
— the pathway for STEM, engineering, sciences, commerce, and most competitive university programs
Foundations of Mathematics 11 & 12
— strong for social sciences, some arts, and programs that don't require calculus
Workplace Mathematics 11 & 12
— for trades and direct-to-work pathways
The streams are not just "harder" versus "easier" — they teach different things. Pre-Calculus is the one that leads toward
Calculus 12
and university calculus, and it's the prerequisite universities look for in science, engineering, and business admission.
Here's where understanding matters more than memorising. Pre-Calculus 12 introduces the tools you'll lean on constantly at UBC or SFU. For example, transformations of functions:
g(x) = a · f(b(x − h)) + k
Where
a
stretches/reflects vertically,
b
stretches/reflects horizontally,
h
shifts left/right, and
k
shifts up/down. Students who
memorise
which letter does what fall apart when the exam mixes them; students who
understand
the geometry sail through.
Logarithms are another Pre-Calc 12 topic where the gap shows:
logb(x) = y  ⟺  bʸ = x
And the change-of-base identity that unlocks half the tricky questions:
logb(x) = (log x) / (log b)
If these already look shaky, that's the signal to reinforce the foundation
before
Grade 12, not during it. This is precisely the kind of concept gap our
Pre-Calculus and math tutoring
is designed to diagnose and close. Small gaps in Grade 10 compound into big struggles in Grade 12 — and a shaky Pre-Calc 12 grade can quietly cap your university options.

Choosing Your Sciences: Physics, Chemistry, Biology — and What Each Unlocks
After
Science 10
, students choose from Grade 11 sciences — typically
Life Sciences 11 (Biology)
Chemistry 11
Physics 11
, and
Earth Sciences 11
— then decide which to continue into Grade 12.
What you take depends heavily on your intended field:
Health sciences, medicine, dentistry, pharmacy
— usually want Biology 12
and
Chemistry 12, often Physics 11 or 12
Engineering
— Physics 12 and Chemistry 12, with Pre-Calculus 12 as the non-negotiable partner
Life sciences, kinesiology, nursing
— Biology 12 and Chemistry 12 are the core
Computer science, math, physics
— Physics 12 and heavy math
A common mistake is dropping a science too early to protect a grade point average, then discovering the target program required it. Always check the specific program before cutting a science.
The sciences reward understanding over cramming even more than math does. Take
Chemistry 11 stoichiometry
— the topic students most often try to survive by plugging numbers into a formula:
moles = (mass in grams) / (molar mass in g/mol)
And the mole ratio that makes balanced equations actually mean something:
For 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O, the ratio of H₂ to H₂O is 2 : 2 = 1 : 1
Or
Physics 11 kinematics
, where students memorise four equations and never know which to reach for:
v = v₀ + a·t
Δx = v₀·t + ½·a·t²
The student who understands that these describe
the same motion from different starting information
chooses the right equation instantly. The one who memorised them freezes. That difference is the whole reason our
science tutoring in Physics, Chemistry, and Biology
leads with the
why
behind each concept.
And if a student is heading toward a health or life-science degree,
Organic Chemistry
looms in Grade 12 and first-year university — a subject where memorising reactions fails hardest and understanding mechanisms wins.
Planning Backward From University: What UBC and SFU Actually Require
The smartest
course selection guidance in BC
starts at the destination and works backward. Instead of asking "What courses should I take?", ask "What does my target program require — and what makes an applicant competitive?"
Both
UBC
and
SFU

typically require, at minimum, English Studies 12 (or equivalent) and a set of approved Grade 12 courses. Most programs also require specific prerequisites — for example, Pre-Calculus 12 for science, engineering, and commerce; particular Grade 12 sciences for health and life-science degrees.
Admission is competitive, and the average of your Grade 11 and 12 admission courses matters a great deal. That's why the strategy is never just "take hard courses" — it's "take the
required
courses and perform well in them." A weak grade in a course you didn't strictly need can pull down an average the program does count.
A practical planning routine we recommend to families:
Pick two or three target programs (even loosely).
Look up each program's
specific
admission requirements on the university's official admissions site.
List every required Grade 11 and 12 course across all of them.
Build a course plan that satisfies the union of those requirements — keeping options open.
Identify which courses need the most support, and reinforce those foundations early.

Because requirements shift over time, always confirm against the university's current official pages rather than older advice. And if you're weighing whether an AP, IB, or extra science is worth it, decide based on your target program's realities — not on what "looks impressive." Our team can help you map this out; that's a normal conversation to start on our
contact page
Timing and Sequencing: Building Each Year So the Next One Isn't a Fresh Panic

Course selection isn't a single decision — it's a three-year sequence where each year sets up the next. Get the order right and Grade 12 feels manageable. Get it wrong and every course becomes a scramble.
A few principles that hold across most Metro Vancouver students:
Protect your prerequisite chains.
Pre-Calculus 10 → 11 → 12 is a chain; a weak link early makes every later link harder. The same is true for the science sequences. Reinforce
before
the gap compounds, not after the report card.

Spreading demanding courses across Grades 11 and 12 protects both your understanding and your grades. Cramming Physics 12, Chemistry 12, Calculus 12, and Pre-Calc 12 into one year with no foundation is how confident students burn out.

The best time to fix a shaky algebra foundation is long before Pre-Calc 12 depends on it. Early support is cheaper, calmer, and far more effective than emergency exam-week tutoring. Our
exam and test preparation program

Some students thrive with in-person, focused sessions in Burnaby; others prefer online tutoring that fits around a packed schedule across Vancouver, Coquitlam, Richmond, or Surrey. Both can work — the right choice is the one the student will actually stick with.
How a PhD-Led Practice Approaches Course Planning Differently
Most tutoring shows up
after
a bad grade to drill the symptom. Our approach is different, and it starts earlier. We diagnose the
concept gaps
behind the grade — the small, compounding foundation issues that make a whole stream feel impossible — and we build understanding that carries forward.
Applied to course selection, that means we don't just tell you which box to tick. We ask:

Is this student genuinely ready for the Pre-Calculus stream, or are there Grade 9–10 gaps that will sabotage it? Do they understand the chemistry well enough to add Chemistry 12, or are they memorising their way through Chem 11?

The PhD leads and oversees the practice; the goal is always the same: real comprehension, so the next concept isn't a fresh panic.

That combination — a genuinely different, understanding-first method plus full-subject coverage under one roof — is what lets us give course guidance that's honest about readiness, not just optimistic about ambition.
Putting It All Together: Your Simple Course-Selection Checklist
Before you lock in next year's courses, walk through this:
Have you confirmed the
Dogwood graduation requirements
are covered?
Have you checked the
specific admission requirements
for two or three target UBC/SFU programs?
Are you in the
right math stream
(Pre-Calculus for STEM/commerce)?
Do your
Grade 12 sciences
match your intended field?
Are demanding courses
spread sensibly
across Grades 11 and 12?
Are there
foundation gaps
to close
now
, before they compound?

support plan
for the courses most likely to be challenging?
If you answered "not sure" to more than one of these, that's completely normal — and it's exactly the moment guidance helps most.
Ready to Build a Course Plan You Feel Confident About?

Course selection shouldn't feel like a guessing game with your child's future. With a clear map of BC graduation requirements, university prerequisites, and the foundations behind each course, you can choose with confidence instead of crossed fingers.

how

Structure

The Mole: The Concept Everything Else Stands On

If we had to name the single gap that quietly wrecks IB Chemistry grades, it's a shaky grasp of the mole. Nearly every calculation in the course — stoichiometry, concentration, gas laws, titrations, energetics — runs through it.
The core relationship students need to
own

n = m / M
Where n is amount in moles, m is mass in grams, and M is molar mass in g·mol⁻¹. Simple on the surface — but the exam tests whether you can
deploy
it under pressure.

Equilibrium is where a lot of HL students hit a wall, because it demands you hold several ideas in your head at once. Consider the general reversible reaction:

An ICE table (Initial, Change, Equilibrium) is the tool that makes these problems tractable, and it's exactly the kind of structured method we teach explicitly rather than leaving students to absorb by osmosis. Organic chemistry is the topic students most often try to

The better way in is to understand that organic reactions are, at heart, about where electrons are and where they want to go. Nucleophiles (electron-rich) attack electrophiles (electron-poor). Once a student sees a reaction as a story of electron movement rather than a random fact to memorise, whole families of mechanisms — substitution, addition, elimination — start to make sense together instead of one at a time.

The Internal Assessment is worth a significant chunk of the final IB Chemistry grade, yet it's where many capable students leave marks on the table — not because the chemistry is hard, but because they don't understand what the rubric rewards.

A strong IA needs a focused, answerable research question, a clearly controlled methodology, honest treatment of uncertainty, and genuine evaluation. That last part — critically evaluating limitations and suggesting realistic improvements — is where students who treat the IA as a formality lose easy marks.
Uncertainty analysis in particular intimidates students. A quick, useful rule for combining percentage uncertainties when you multiply or divide measurements:
total % uncertainty ≈ %Δ₁ + %Δ₂ + %Δ₃ ...

So if you measure mass with 2% uncertainty and volume with 3% uncertainty and divide them, your result carries roughly 5% uncertainty. Small, teachable skill — meaningful mark difference. Here's a scene we see almost every week. A student sits down for three hours the night before a Chem 11 test. They re-read the notes. They highlight. They flip flashcards. And the next morning, the moment the exam lands on the desk, the fog rolls in — and everything they "knew" evaporates.
The parents' conclusion is usually, "He just needs to study more." But the truth is almost always the opposite. The problem isn't the
amount
of studying — it's the
method

. Re-reading and highlighting feel productive, but the research on how memory actually works tells us they're some of the weakest ways to learn. The student worked hard and still walked out frustrated. That's not a motivation problem. That's a skills problem — and study skills can be taught.
That's what
study skills coaching
is. Not a lecture about "trying harder," and not another pile of homework. It's teaching a student
how to learn

— how to encode information so it sticks, how to test themselves honestly, how to spot the concept gaps that keep tripping them up, and how to walk into an exam calm instead of foggy. At Dr. Shreyank Educare, this runs through everything we do, whether you're with us
in person in Burnaby or online across Metro Vancouver

Concept Gaps vs. Practice Gaps: The Distinction That Changes Everything
When a student is stuck, there are really only two things going wrong, and they need completely different fixes.
A
practice gap
means the student understands the idea but hasn't done it enough times for it to feel automatic. The fix is straightforward: more well-designed practice. A
concept gap
is different — it means something
underneath
the current topic never fully clicked, and that shaky foundation is quietly sabotaging everything built on top of it.
Here's why this matters so much: concept gaps
compound

. A student who never truly understood how fractions relate to division will struggle with ratios, then with slope, then with rates of change in Calculus 12 at UBC or SFU — and every teacher along the way will think it's a "new" problem. It isn't. It's the same tiny gap, wearing a bigger costume each year.
Good study skills coaching starts by diagnosing
which

gap you're actually dealing with. Drilling practice problems at a concept gap is like repainting a wall with a crack running through it — it looks better for a week, then the crack shows again. This diagnostic-first approach is the heart of our
understanding-first method
, and it's why we spend the first session listening and probing before we ever assign a worksheet.
Why Memorisation Fails — and What to Do Instead

Memorisation feels safe. You either know it or you don't, and cramming gives you the comforting illusion of a full tank. But memorisation stores facts as isolated islands with no bridges between them. Under exam pressure, when you need to
retrieve
one, there's no path to find it.
Understanding builds the bridges. When you know
why
a formula works, you can rebuild it even if you blank on the exact form. Take kinematics in Physics 11. A student who memorises this equation:
v² = v₀² + 2·a·Δx
...has one brittle fact. A student who
understands

it knows it comes from combining velocity and displacement — that it's the tool you reach for when you have distance but no time. That student can adapt when the problem is phrased sideways. Same equation, completely different security.
Or consider a genetics cross in Biology 12. Memorising "9:3:3:1" is fragile. Understanding
why
a dihybrid cross of two heterozygotes produces:
9 : 3 : 3 : 1  (from a 3:1 ratio multiplied by a 3:1 ratio)
...means you can rebuild the ratio from scratch, and adjust it when a question changes the parental genotypes. The memoriser panics; the understander reasons.
This is the shift study skills coaching creates: from
storing
to
reasoning
. It's slower for the first few weeks and dramatically faster forever after.
The Study Techniques That Actually Move the Needle

Decades of learning science point to a small handful of techniques that outperform everything else. The good news for students in Burnaby and across Metro Vancouver: none of them require talent. They just require knowing what they are and building the habit.
Retrieval practice
— Close the book and try to recall the idea from memory
before
checking. The struggle to retrieve is exactly what strengthens the memory. This is why self-quizzing beats re-reading every single time.
Spaced repetition
— Instead of one three-hour cram, do six 30-minute sessions across two weeks. The same total time, spread out, produces far stronger retention because each review reactivates a fading memory.
Interleaving
— Mix problem types rather than doing 20 of the same kind in a row. It feels harder (and it is), but it trains the brain to
choose
the right method — which is exactly what an exam demands.
Self-explanation
— After solving a problem, say out loud
why
each step works. If you can't explain it, you've found your concept gap.
Worked-example study
— Study a fully solved problem slowly, then reproduce it from blank. This scaffolds understanding before independent practice.

Notice that the two techniques students love most — re-reading and highlighting — aren't on this list. They feel good precisely because they're easy, and easy is the opposite of what builds durable learning. A good coach makes the productive-but-harder methods feel doable, and holds the student accountable to them.

Every student knows the fog — that moment when a mind that felt prepared suddenly goes blank. It's not a character flaw and it's not rare. It's your working memory getting hijacked by stress, leaving less room for the actual problem in front of you.

The fix is partly emotional and partly structural. Emotionally, deep, slow breathing before and during a test genuinely lowers the stress response — it's not a cliché, it's physiology. Structurally, the antidote is

children.text: Why the Smartest Students Still Run Out of Time

Here's something we see almost every week at our Burnaby practice: a genuinely capable student, sitting down with three assignments, a Chem 11 test on Thursday, soccer at 6, and a phone buzzing every ninety seconds. They're not lazy. They're not incapable. They've simply never been
taught
how to manage time — because almost no one is.

Time management is treated like something you're supposed to absorb by osmosis. In reality, it's a skill with its own techniques, just like factoring a quadratic or balancing a redox equation. And when that skill is missing, it quietly sabotages everything else. A student who understands Pre-Calc 12 perfectly can still bomb the unit test because they left studying until 10 p.m. the night before, ran into a concept gap, panicked, and never recovered.
That's the insight most people miss. Poor grades often aren't a knowledge problem
or
a discipline problem — they're a
time-and-planning problem

The Hidden Math of a Student's Week
Parents are often shocked when we actually count the hours. Let's do it, because the numbers are genuinely revealing.
A week has 168 hours. Start subtracting:
168 − (8 hrs sleep × 7) = 168 − 56 = 112 hrs awake
112 − (school + commute ≈ 40) = 72 hrs
72 − (meals, chores, hygiene ≈ 21) = 51 hrs
51 − (sports, family, downtime ≈ 25) = 26 hrs for homework + study

Twenty-six hours sounds like plenty — until you split it across five or six courses, add a part-time job, and account for the reality that focused study is far more tiring than passive scrolling. Suddenly that buffer evaporates.
The lesson isn't "do more." It's that time is a genuinely
finite, measurable resource
— and once students see it as a budget rather than an endless stream, they start spending it deliberately. Good time management coaching begins here: making the invisible visible.
Concept Gaps Steal Time — And Compound Like Interest

This is where our understanding-first method connects directly to the clock. When a student has a small unresolved concept gap — say, they never fully understood how to isolate a variable — every single homework question in that unit takes
longer
, feels
harder
, and drains
more
willpower than it should.
Think of it like compound interest working against you:
Time lost ≈ basetime × (1 + gappenalty)ⁿ

where n is the number of topics built on that shaky foundation. In Pre-Calculus 12, a wobbly grasp of function transformations makes trigonometry harder, which makes the eventual Calculus 12 or first-year UBC/SFU calculus course a genuine struggle. The gap didn't just cost one bad test — it taxed months of study time.
This is why we never separate study skills from actual subject mastery. Fixing the
why

behind a concept is one of the biggest time-savers there is. A student who truly understands stoichiometry doesn't need to re-learn it before every Chem 11 quiz — they recall it in a fraction of the time. If you'd like to see how we diagnose those gaps, our
science tutoring programs
are built entirely around this principle.
The Coaching Method: From Overwhelm to a System That Runs Itself
So what does time management coaching for students actually look like in practice? It's not lecturing a teenager to "just be more organised." It's building a system
with
them, tuned to how they really live. Here's the core of our approach.
1. Map the real week, not the ideal one

We start by tracking where the hours genuinely go for a few days. Almost every student discovers a "leak" — usually 60–90 minutes of fragmented phone time they didn't feel happening. We don't shame it; we redesign around it.
2. Estimate honestly, then add a buffer
Students chronically underestimate how long tasks take — psychologists call it the planning fallacy. We coach a simple correction:
realistictime ≈ firstestimate × 1.5
That 1.5 multiplier turns "I'll do it in twenty minutes" (and then it's midnight) into a plan that actually holds.
3. Work in focused blocks

Sustained focus fades fast. We use timed blocks — often 25 to 40 minutes of deep work followed by a short, deliberate break. This isn't a gimmick; it matches how attention actually cycles, and it makes starting far less daunting.
4. Sequence by leverage, not by anxiety
Students naturally do the easy, comforting task first. We flip that: tackle the highest-leverage work — the tricky Physics 12 problem set, the essay outline — when energy is freshest.
Here's the short version of the toolkit we build with every student:
A single home base
— one planner or calendar, not five apps and three sticky notes
Weekly planning ritual
— ten minutes every Sunday to look at the week ahead
Task breakdown
— turning "study for Bio" into three specific, finishable actions
Buffer time
— deliberate empty slots for the assignment that always runs long
A shutdown routine
— a clear end to the study day, so rest is real rest

Managing the Fog Before the Exam

Every BC student knows the feeling: the fog that rolls in the night before a big test. Provincial numeracy assessments, AP exams, IB internals, the SAT — the stakes feel enormous and the brain goes blank.
Here's the honest truth: last-minute cramming doesn't just feel bad, it's
inefficient time-spending

. Memory research is consistent on this — the same total study hours spread across days produce far better recall than the same hours packed into one panicked night. This is called spaced practice, and it's the single most time-effective study strategy there is.
A simple version we teach:
Review at day 1 → day 3 → day 7 → day 14
Each review takes less time than the last, because the material is settling into long-term memory. A student who spaces their Chem 11 review over two weeks spends
fewer

total hours and walks in calmer than the one who pulled an all-nighter. That's the whole promise of time management coaching: not more work, but work that finally pays off. For subject-specific exam strategy, our

Balancing School, Sports, and a Life in Metro Vancouver

Students in Burnaby, Vancouver, Coquitlam, Surrey, and across the region are busy in ways that are genuinely admirable — competitive sports, music, volunteering, part-time jobs, family responsibilities. We would never tell a student to drop the things that make them who they are.
Good time management is what

What Changes When Students Actually Own Their Time

The grades matter — of course they do. But the change we're proudest of is quieter. A student who used to say "I'm just bad at managing my time" starts saying "I've got this handled." That shift in identity is the real outcome, and it lasts far longer than any single test.

children.text: Why Post-Secondary Planning in Vancouver Starts Earlier Than Most Families Think
Here's the quiet truth about post secondary planning Vancouver families discover — usually too late: the doors to UBC, SFU, UVic, BCIT, and beyond aren't decided in Grade 12. They're decided in the
choices
made in Grade 10 and 11, and in the
foundations
built years before that.

By the time a Grade 12 student sits down to apply, the prerequisite courses are locked in, the grades that matter are largely already earned, and the concept gaps that quietly capped a Chemistry or Pre-Calculus mark have long since compounded. Planning isn't a Grade 12 event. It's a three-year arc — and the earlier a family maps it, the more options stay open.

We're a PhD-led tutoring practice based in Burnaby, working with students in-person and online across Metro Vancouver — Vancouver, New Westminster, Coquitlam, Richmond, Surrey, and North Vancouver. Over the years we've noticed the same pattern again and again: the student who struggles with UBC admission isn't lacking ability. They're carrying small, unaddressed concept gaps that made a required course harder than it needed to be.
This guide walks you through the real roadmap — which courses matter, what BC's post-secondary institutions actually ask for, and how to plan so your teen keeps the widest range of choices possible.

— no pressure, just an honest read on where the gaps are.
The BC Course Map: What UBC and SFU Are Really Looking For
Let's get concrete, because vague advice helps no one.
Most Metro Vancouver students enter post-secondary through the
BC secondary school diploma (Dogwood)
, which requires 80 credits, including specific Grade 10–12 courses and the provincial Numeracy and Literacy Graduation Assessments. But graduating is not the same as being
competitive
for the program you want.
For
UBC
and
SFU
, general admission looks at your Grade 11 and 12 courses, with particular weight on the courses relevant to your intended program. A few realities that shape planning:
English Studies 12
(or English First Peoples 12) is required across the board.
Many science and engineering programs require
Pre-Calculus 12
— and often
Chemistry 12
and
Physics 12
as well.
Life-science and health pathways lean on
Biology 12
and
Chemistry 12
Commerce and quantitative programs want strong
Pre-Calculus 12
, and Calculus 12 is a genuine advantage even when it's not strictly required.
Faculties admit on an
approximate admission average
built from your relevant Grade 12 courses — so a weak grade in a required course carries real weight.
The planning move here is simple but overlooked:
work backwards from the program, not forwards from the timetable.

If your teen might want engineering at UBC or a science pathway at SFU, Pre-Calculus 12 and the sciences aren't optional electives to squeeze in — they're the spine of the plan, and each one has prerequisite courses in Grade 11 that must come first.
If your student is aiming at these programs, our
high school Grades 8–12 support
is built around exactly these prerequisite chains — making sure Chem 11 is solid
before
Chem 12 turns into a fog.
The Real Reason Students Fall Behind: Concept Gaps That Compound

Here's the insight most tutoring skips over. When a capable student's grade slips in Pre-Calc 12 or Chemistry 12, the problem usually isn't Grade 12 material. It's a small gap from a year or two earlier that never got addressed — and now everything built on top of it wobbles.

Consider a student struggling with logarithms in Pre-Calculus 12. Nine times out of ten, the real issue is that exponent rules from Grade 10 were memorised, not understood. The moment logs appear, the foundation gives way. If you don't genuinely grasp that
logₐ(x) = y  ⟺  aʸ = x
then the change-of-base formula
logₐ(x) = (log x) / (log a)
is just another string of symbols to survive. Understand the first line and the second becomes obvious.

The same pattern shows up in Chemistry 12. Students hit equilibrium and reaction rates and panic — but the actual gap is often stoichiometry from Chem 11. If setting up mole ratios still feels shaky, then an equilibrium expression like
never really clicks; it's memorised and forgotten by exam day.
And in Physics 12, the classic wall is kinematics — because the algebra underneath it was never comfortable. A student who can confidently rearrange
v² = v₀² + 2·a·Δx
to solve for acceleration is doing Grade 10 algebra, not Grade 12 physics. When the algebra is automatic, the physics becomes learnable.
This is why effective post-secondary planning isn't just about scheduling the right courses. It's about
diagnosing and closing the concept gaps
before
they cap a grade that admissions will read. Our
science tutoring
— Physics, Chemistry, and Biology — is built around finding that root gap, not just drilling this week's worksheet.
Want to know which gap is quietly costing your teen marks?
Book a free assessment
— we'll pinpoint it and show you the plan, with zero pressure to sign up.
Grade-by-Grade: Your Metro Vancouver Planning Timeline
Post-secondary planning works best when it's a rhythm, not a scramble. Here's a realistic year-by-year arc for Metro Vancouver families.
Grade 9–10: Build the Foundation

This is where the invisible groundwork happens. Algebra fluency, fraction and exponent confidence, and solid reading and writing habits set the ceiling for everything that follows. Grades here rarely go on a university application — but the
understanding
built here decides whether Grade 11 and 12 feel manageable or overwhelming.
Grade 11: Choose Deliberately

Grade 11 is the year to lock in the prerequisite courses your target programs need — Pre-Calculus 11, Chemistry 11, Physics 11, Biology 11 — and to take them seriously, because they gate the Grade 12 versions. Some faculties look at select Grade 11 grades too. Start browsing UBC, SFU, and BCIT program pages now, together as a family.
Grade 12: Execute and Apply

This is when the relevant Grade 12 courses, provincial assessments, and applications all land. Application timelines for many BC institutions open in the fall of Grade 12, so autumn is busy. This is a poor time to
discover
a concept gap — which is exactly why the earlier work matters. It's also the year for
exam and test preparation
to shine, from provincials to program-specific requirements.
Considering the SAT?
Some students apply to U.S. or international schools, or use the SAT to strengthen a profile. If that's on the table, our
SAT preparation classes
cover both the Math and the Reading & Writing sections — but plan the timeline early, since it competes for attention with Grade 12 coursework.
In-Person in Burnaby or Online Across Metro Vancouver: Choosing What Fits
One practical planning question we hear constantly:
should tutoring be in-person or online?
Both work well — the right choice depends on the student.

In-person sessions at our Burnaby location suit students who focus better with someone physically beside them, or who are working through hands-on problem sets in Physics and Chemistry. Online sessions across Metro Vancouver — Vancouver, Coquitlam, Richmond, Surrey, New West, North Van — remove the commute entirely and often make consistent weekly scheduling far easier for busy families.
What
doesn't
change between the two is the method: one-on-one, understanding-first, focused on the
why

behind each step so the next concept isn't a fresh panic. Whether your teen is preparing for a UBC science pathway or catching up in Pre-Calc 11, the approach is the same — diagnose the gap, teach for real comprehension, build confidence that survives exam day.
Beyond the Grades: The Confidence That Actually Carries Into University
Post-secondary planning tends to fixate on numbers — averages, prerequisites, admission cut-offs. Those matter. But the students who
thrive
once they arrive at UBC, SFU, or BCIT share something the transcript doesn't show: they learned how to learn.

First-year university math and science move fast. A student who got through Grade 12 by memorising hits a wall when UBC calculus or first-year chemistry assumes genuine understanding. The student who built real foundations — who understands
why
the quadratic formula works, not just how to plug into it — adapts.
That discriminant, b² − 4ac, tells you
how many real solutions exist before you even solve

— negative means none, zero means one, positive means two. A student who understands that isn't just passing Grade 11; they're building the kind of thinking university rewards. If your teen is already looking at first-year courses, our
college and post-secondary course help
supports that transition directly.
That's the real goal of good planning: not just
getting in
, but
being ready.
For Adult Learners: Post-Secondary Planning Is for You Too

Post-secondary planning in Vancouver isn't only for teenagers. Plenty of adult learners return to upgrade — completing a Chemistry 12 or Pre-Calculus 12 they never finished, meeting a prerequisite for a nursing or trades or business program, or rebuilding math confidence after years away.
The same principle applies, often even more so: the barrier is usually a specific concept gap, not a lack of ability. Our
adult academic upgrading
meets you where you are — patiently, without judgment, and around a working schedule.
Putting It All Together: A Simple Planning Checklist
Here's a distilled starting point for any Metro Vancouver family beginning the process:
Identify 2–3 target programs
and read their actual prerequisite and admission-average requirements on the UBC, SFU, or BCIT websites.
Map the prerequisite chain backwards
— which Grade 11 courses gate the required Grade 12 courses.
Audit for concept gaps now
, not in Grade 12 — a shaky algebra or stoichiometry foundation will quietly cap otherwise-good grades.
Decide in-person vs online
based on how your student focuses best.
Build a consistent weekly rhythm
rather than crisis-mode cramming before each exam.
Done early, none of this is stressful. Done late, all of it is. The whole point of planning is to trade a frantic Grade 12 for a calm, deliberate three years.

Frequently Asked Questions
When should we start post-secondary planning in Vancouver?

Ideally in Grade 9 or 10. The Grade 11 and 12 course choices that gate UBC and SFU programs depend on foundations built earlier, and concept gaps from Grade 10 often quietly cap Grade 12 grades. Starting early keeps the most options open — but it's never too late to make a real plan.
What Grade 12 courses do UBC and SFU require?

English Studies 12 (or English First Peoples 12) is required across programs. Science, engineering, and quantitative pathways typically require Pre-Calculus 12, often with Chemistry 12 and Physics 12; life-science routes lean on Biology 12 and Chemistry 12. Always check the exact prerequisites on the specific program's page, as they vary by faculty.
Is online tutoring as effective as in-person for exam prep?

Yes — both work well, and the method is identical: one-on-one, understanding-first teaching. In-person in Burnaby suits students who focus better beside a tutor; online across Metro Vancouver removes the commute and makes consistent weekly sessions easier. The best choice depends on how your student learns.
My teen has good grades but panics on exams — is that a concept gap?

Often, yes. Exam panic frequently signals material that was memorised rather than truly understood — it holds up on homework but collapses under time pressure. A free assessment can pinpoint whether the issue is a genuine concept gap or exam strategy, so we address the real cause.
